We are 3DC, a team of four passionate Computer Engineering students: Matteo D'Onofrio, Fabrizio D'Errico, Emanuel Chirico, and Aniello De Girolamo Del Mauro. With three members specializing in Embedded Systems and one in Cybersecurity, we combine our technical skills, creativity, and passion for innovation to tackle real-world challenges. Our mission is to transform ambitious ideas into impactful technological solutions, pushing the boundaries of engineering.
summary:
S.L.O.T.H. is an AI companion and mission-support dashboard designed to help astronauts communicate and monitor their daily wellbeing. It addresses the challenge “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions,” focusing on isolation and confinement and distance from Earth.

The prototype combines voice or text check-ins about sleep, fatigue and physical wellbeing with simulated sensor readings and optional webcam observations of eyelid closures. After the astronaut confirms the information to share, S.L.O.T.H. generates a personalized report for ground control, distinguishing reported experiences, measurements, discrepancies and uncertainty.

When appropriate, the assistant can propose a schedule adjustment, such as a short rest before a flexible activity. Proposals are checked against schedule constraints and require ground-control approval before being applied.

S.L.O.T.H. aims to make wellbeing monitoring more approachable while giving mission operators context that sensor readings alone may miss. Its conversational and journaling features also explore support for reflection during isolation. Informed by NASA Human Research Program resources, the prototype demonstrates a human-supervised workflow; it does not provide medical diagnoses or replace operational expertise.
details:
S.L.O.T.H. is an astronaut wellbeing companion and mission-support dashboard. It combines conversational check-ins, simulated sensor readings and optional webcam observations to help astronauts describe how they feel and give ground control a clearer picture of their daily wellbeing.

The astronaut interacts with the assistant through text or voice, reporting sleep duration, sleep quality, fatigue and physical observations. A webcam feature records eyelid closures during a short observation session, together with measurement quality and limitations. After the astronaut confirms the check-in and selects what to share, the system combines this information with simulated sleep measurements to generate a report for ground control. The report distinguishes self-reported information, sensor readings, webcam observations, discrepancies and uncertainty.

When appropriate, the assistant can propose a bounded schedule adjustment, such as a short rest before a flexible activity. Proposals are checked against schedule constraints and require ground-control approval before they are applied. The dashboard lets operators review reports and proposals, while fictional crew profiles, interactive 3D human models and visual measurements make the information easier to explore.

The intended benefit is to connect measurements with the astronaut’s own experience. Sensor readings alone may miss important context about perceived sleep, discomfort or workload. S.L.O.T.H. provides a conversational way to communicate that context and supports human review rather than automatically making mission decisions. Its companionship and journaling features also explore ways to support reflection during isolation. Any improvement in loneliness, sleep or psychological health remains a hypothesis requiring future evaluation.

We developed the prototype using TypeScript, React and Next.js for the dashboard and agent interface; Python and FastAPI for the data backend; Prisma and SQLite for local persistence; Three.js and React Three Fiber for the 3D body visualization; and MediaPipe for webcam face landmarks and eyelid analysis. The assistant uses a configurable language-model provider, including NVIDIA Nemotron, and text-to-speech for spoken replies. The demonstration runs on a computer with a webcam and microphone. Crew profiles and sensor readings are synthetic; no physical medical sensors are connected.

The creative contribution is the integration of conversation, self-reports, experimental eyelid observations and simulated measurements into a workflow that ends with an understandable report and a reviewable schedule proposal. We considered measurement quality, conflicting information, missing data, consent to share observations, voice-service failures and the importance of preserving human authority.

NASA Human Research Program resources, including 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight, informed our focus on isolation, confinement and distance from Earth. Our scientific foundation document connects research to proposed features and identifies their limits. The prototype is a demonstration, not a validated medical or operational NASA system. AI tools assisted development, synthetic data, visual assets and presentation preparation; their use is disclosed in the project documentation and submission materials.
dataRefs: The Real Story About Astronaut Health Care in Space
